\section[vīgintī annōs nātus sum]{vīgintī annōs nātus sum — a THIRD way to say your age}

\label{lesson:LA-C14-annos-natus}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know that Spanish and French say "I HAVE my years," and German/English say "I AM my years." Here's the honest surprise: Latin itself did \textbf{neither}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vīgintī annōs nātus sum — "twenty years born"}
\textbf{vīgintī annōs nātus sum} = "\textbf{I am twenty years old}" — literally "\textbf{I am, having been born, twenty years}" (a man speaking; a woman says \textbf{nāta}). Taken apart:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{nātus/nāta} — "\textbf{born}," the perfect passive participle of \textbf{nāscor}, "to be born" (the same root behind English \textbf{nature, native, nation, innate}).
  \item \textbf{annōs} — "\textbf{years}," in the \textbf{accusative case}, marking \textbf{duration} — "for twenty years {[}of life so far{]}." This is the same accusative-of-duration you'd use for "I studied \textbf{for three years}" (\emph{trēs annōs}).
  \item \textbf{sum} — "I am."
\end{itemize}

So the whole phrase reads: "I am — having been born {[}and living{]} twenty years {[}so far{]}." Cicero uses exactly this pattern in \emph{Cato Maior de Senectute} (§14), in Cato's own voice: \textbf{quīnque et sexāgintā annōs nātus}, "having been born sixty-\textbf{five} years," i.e., "at sixty-five years old" — the same section also gives Ennius's age as \textbf{annōs septuāgintā nātus}, "seventy."

\begin{culture}
You've already met the clean Romance/Germanic split for this concept — Romance languages \textbf{have} their years (\emph{tengo}, \emph{j'ai}, \emph{ho}), Germanic languages \textbf{are} their years (\emph{ich bin}, \emph{I am}). Here's the twist: \textbf{Latin itself used neither construction.} Classical Latin's \emph{nātus} + accusative-of-duration pattern is a \textbf{third}, distinct grammatical shape — not "having" years, not simply "being" a number, but "being \textbf{born-for-that-long}." The Romance "have your years" pattern (\emph{habēre} + years) that Spanish, French, and Italian all inherited is a \textbf{Vulgar Latin innovation} that arose \textbf{after} Classical Latin, replacing the older \emph{nātus} construction — so Spanish's \emph{tengo veinte años} is NOT a direct continuation of how Cicero would have said it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vīgintī annōs nātus sum" — I am twenty years old, literally "born twenty years"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "nātus" — born, same root as English "native, nature, nation"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest surprise — this is a THIRD pattern, neither "have" nor simple "be"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{vīgintī annōs nātus sum} literally mean? ("I am, having been \textbf{born}, twenty years" — using the perfect participle \emph{nātus} + the accusative of duration.) Does this match Romance's "have your years" pattern? (\textbf{No} — that's a \textbf{later Vulgar Latin innovation}, not what Classical Latin did.) What English words share the root of \emph{nātus}? (\textbf{Native, nature, nation, innate}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
